title: Hesiod came long after Moses
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος ἐκτιθέμενος τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἔξω τοῦ θείου λόγου ἱστορίας, τὰ περὶ τῶν ἐπιδικασαμένων ἀνθρώπων τῆς ἀρχαιότητος, οἷον Ἀθηναίων καὶ Αἰγυπτίων καὶ Ἀρκάδων καὶ Φρυγῶν, καὶ γηγενεῖς τινας παρὰ σφίσιν γεγονέναι λεγόντων καὶ τεκμήρια τούτων παρεχομένων ἑκάστων, φησὶν ὡς ἄρα Ἰουδαῖοι ἐν γωνίᾳ που τῆς Παλαιστίνης συγκύψαντες, παντελῶς ἀπαίδευτοι καὶ οὐ προακηκοότες πάλαι ταῦτα Ἡσιόδῳ καὶ ἄλλοις μυρίοις ἀνδράσιν ἐνθέοις ὑμνημένα, συνέθεσαν ἀπιθανώτατα καὶ ἀμουσότατα, ἄνθρωπόν τινα ὑπὸ χειρῶν θεοῦ πλασσόμενόν τε καὶ ἐμφυσώμενον καὶ γύναιον ἐκ τῆς πλευρᾶς καὶ παραγγέλματα τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ὄφιν τούτοις ἀντιπράσσοντα καὶ περιγινόμενον τῶν θεοῦ προσταγμάτων τὸν ὄφιν, μῦθόν τινα ὡς γραυσὶ διηγούμενοι καὶ ποιοῦντες ἀνοσιώτατα τὸν θεὸν, εὐθὺς ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς ἀσθενοῦντα καὶ μηδ᾿ ἕν᾿ ἄνθρωπον, ὃν αὐτὸς ἔπλασε, πεῖσαι δυνάμενον. διὰ τούτων δὴ ὁ πολυΐστωρ καὶ πολυμαθὴς καὶ Ἰουδαίοις καὶ Χριστιανοῖς ἀμαθίαν ἐγκαλῶν καὶ ἀπαιδευσίαν Κέλσος σαφῶς παρίστησι, τίνα τρόπον ἀκριβῶς ᾔδει τοὺς ἑκάστου συγγραφέως χρόνους, Ἕλληνος καὶ βαρβάρου· ὅς γε οἴεται Ἡσίοδον καὶ ἄλλους μυρίους. οὓς ὀνομάζει ἄνδρας ἐνθέους. πρεσβυτέρους εἶναι Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν τούτου γραμμάτων. Μωϋσέως, τοῦ ἀποδεικνυμένου πολλῷ τῶν Ἰλιακῶν πρεσβυτέρου. οὐκ Ἰουδαῖοι οὖν συνέθεσαν ἀπιθανώτατα καὶ ἀμουσότατα τὰ περὶ τὸν γηγενῆ ἄνθρωπον, ἀλλ᾿ οἱ κατὰ Κέλσον ἄνδρες ἔνθεοι, Ἡσίοδος καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι αὐτοῦ μυρίοι, τοὺς πολλῷ πρεσβυτέρους καὶ σεμνοτάτους ἐν τῇ Παλαιστίνῃ λόγους μήτε μαθόντες μήτ᾿ ἀκηκοότες. τοιαύτας ἔγραψαν ἱστορίας περὶ τῶν ἀρχαίων. ὁποίας καὶ θεογονίας. γένεσιν τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς περιτιθέντες θεοῖς. καὶ ἄλλα μυρία. εὐλόγως (οὖν) ἐκβάλλει τῆς ἑαυτοῦ πολιτείας Πλάτων ὡς ἐπιτρίβοντας τοὺς νέους τὸν Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς τοιαῦτα γράφοντας ποιήματα. ἀλλὰ Πλάτων μὲν δῆλός ἐστι μὴ φρονήσας ἐνθέους γεγονέναι ἄνδρας τοὺς τοιαῦτα ποιήματα καταλελοιπότας· ὁ δὲ κρίνειν μᾶλλον Πλάτωνος δυνάμενος, ὁ Ἐπικούρειος Κέλσος. εἴ γε οὗτός ἐστι καὶ ὁ κατὰ Χριστιανῶν ἄλλα δύο βιβλία συντάξας, τάχα ἡμῖν φιλονεικῶν οὓς μὴ ἐφρόνει ἐνθέους ἐνθέους ὠνόμασεν.
pass_a_gloss: After these things Celsus, setting out (ἐκτιθέμενος) things from the history outside (ἔξω) the divine word (θείου λόγου), things about men who laid claim (ἐπιδικασαμένων) to antiquity (ἀρχαιότητος), such as Athenians, Egyptians, Arcadians, Phrygians, saying that certain earth-born (γηγενεῖς) [men] arose among them and each presenting proofs (τεκμήρια) of these, says that 'Jews, huddled together (συγκύψαντες) in some corner (γωνίᾳ) of Palestine, entirely uneducated (ἀπαίδευτοι) and not having heard beforehand (προακηκοότες) these things long ago hymned (ὑμνημένα) by Hesiod and countless (μυρίοις) other inspired (ἐνθέοις) men, composed (συνέθεσαν) most unpersuasively (ἀπιθανώτατα) and most tastelessly (ἀμουσότατα) a man being moulded (πλασσόμενον) by hands of God and being blown into (ἐμφυσώμενον), and a little woman (γύναιον) from the side (πλευρᾶς), and precepts (παραγγέλματα) of God, and a serpent (ὄφιν) acting against (ἀντιπράσσοντα) these and the serpent prevailing over (περιγινόμενον) God's commands (προσταγμάτων), narrating a myth (μῦθον) as to old women (γραυσί) and making God most unholily (ἀνοσιώτατα) weak (ἀσθενοῦντα) straight from the beginning and unable to persuade (πεῖσαι) even one man whom he himself moulded (ἔπλασε).' Through these the much-informed (πολυΐστωρ) and much-learned (πολυμαθής) Celsus, charging Jews and Christians with ignorance (ἀμαθίαν) and lack of education (ἀπαιδευσίαν), clearly shows in what manner he accurately knew the times (χρόνους) of each writer, Greek and barbarian; who thinks Hesiod and countless others, whom he names inspired men, older (πρεσβυτέρους) than Moses and his writings, Moses who is demonstrated (ἀποδεικνυμένου) much older than the Trojan matters (Ἰλιακῶν). Not Jews then composed most unpersuasively and tastelessly the things about the earth-born man, but the men inspired according to Celsus, Hesiod and his countless others, neither having learned nor heard the much older and most venerable (σεμνοτάτους) accounts (λόγους) in Palestine, wrote such histories about the ancients, such as theogonies (θεογονίας) too, attributing (περιτιθέντες), so far as in them lay (τὸ ὅσον ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς), birth (γένεσιν) to gods, and countless other things. Reasonably (εὐλόγως) [then] Plato expels (ἐκβάλλει) from his commonwealth (πολιτείας) Homer and those writing such poems as corrupting (ἐπιτρίβοντας) the young. But Plato is clear (δῆλος) not having thought (φρονήσας) those who left such poems to have been inspired men; but the one more able to judge (κρίνειν) than Plato, the Epicurean Celsus, if indeed this is also the one who composed two other books against Christians, perhaps (τάχα) from contentiousness (φιλονεικῶν) toward us named inspired those he did not think inspired.
pass_b_english: After this Celsus sets out material from history outside the divine word, about people who have laid claim to antiquity, such as the Athenians, Egyptians, Arcadians and Phrygians, who say that certain earth-born men arose among them, and each of whom offers proofs of it. And he says that “the Jews, huddled together in some corner of Palestine, utterly uneducated, and not having heard of these things sung long ago by Hesiod and countless other inspired men, put together a most incredible and tasteless tale: a man moulded by the hands of God and blown into (Genesis 2:7), a little woman made from his side (Genesis 2:21–22), commandments of God (Genesis 2:16–17), and a serpent working against these commandments, the serpent getting the better of God’s orders (Genesis 3:1–6). They tell a sort of myth, as if to old women, and most impiously make God weak from the very beginning, unable to persuade even the one man whom he himself had moulded.”

In these words the widely read and learned Celsus, who charges both Jews and Christians with ignorance and lack of education, plainly shows how accurately he knew the dates of each writer, Greek and barbarian! For he thinks that Hesiod and countless others, whom he calls inspired men, are older than Moses and his writings: Moses, who is shown to be much older than the Trojan War.

So it was not the Jews who put together a most incredible and tasteless tale about the earth-born man, but Celsus’s “inspired men”, Hesiod and his countless others. Having neither learned nor heard the far older and most venerable accounts in Palestine, they wrote such histories about the ancients as their theogonies too, ascribing birth to gods, so far as it lay with them, and countless other things.

With good reason, then, Plato expels from his commonwealth Homer and those who write such poems, as corrupters of the young (Plato, Republic 398a; 607a). Plato plainly did not think that those who left such poems behind were inspired men. But Celsus the Epicurean, who is better able to judge than Plato, if indeed he is the same man who composed two other books against the Christians, has perhaps, out of a wish to quarrel with us, called “inspired” those whom he did not think inspired.

choices.choice: 'laid claim to great antiquity' -> 'laid claim to antiquity' (removed added 'great'; τῆς ἀρχαιότητος)
'Then he says' -> 'And he says' (φησίν is the main verb of the same sentence; no 'then' in the Greek)
'a serpent working against them' -> 'a serpent working against these commandments' (τούτοις = the παραγγέλματα; 'them' read as the humans)
'unable to persuade even one man, whom he himself had moulded' -> 'even the one man whom he himself had moulded' (μηδ' ἕνα ... ὃν αὐτὸς ἔπλασε, restrictive)

Celsus's words kept in double quotation marks and the attribution 'he says' kept; Genesis 2:7, 2:16-17, 2:21-22, 3:1-6 checked against the narrative; Plato, Republic 398a and 607a checked (poet sent away; only hymns and praises admitted, Homer named at 606e-607a); kept

Celsus's words run from 'the Jews, huddled together' to 'whom he himself had moulded'; Origen gives them in indirect speech after φησὶν ὡς ἄρα and they are rendered as a direct quotation. The Genesis citations inside the quotation mark Celsus's paraphrase of Genesis 2–3, not verbatim quotation. Celsus's 'ἐμφυσώμενον' is rendered 'blown into' (not 'breathed into') to prepare Origen's wineskin retort in 4.37. 'γύναιον' is contemptuous diminutive ('a little woman'). 'μῦθόν τινα ὡς γραυσὶ διηγούμενοι' = 'a myth such as one tells old women'; the old-wives'-tale idea recalls 1 Timothy 4:7 (γραώδεις μύθους), but the words are Celsus's and no allusion is cited. 'τῶν Ἰλιακῶν' = the events at Troy, rendered 'the Trojan War'. Plato's expulsion of Homer and the imitative poets: Republic 398a (the poet sent away to another city) and 607a (only hymns to the gods and praises of good men admitted); the phrase 'corrupting the young' is Origen's summary. The 'two other books against the Christians' follow the staged text (κατὰ Χριστιανῶν); Origen elsewhere (1.8) distinguishes an Epicurean Celsus and is unsure of the identification, hence 'if indeed'. 'ὁ δὲ κρίνειν μᾶλλον Πλάτωνος δυνάμενος' is ironic. 'ὠνόμασεν ἐνθέους' — the staged row repeats ἐνθέους (οὓς μὴ ἐφρόνει ἐνθέους ἐνθέους ὠνόμασεν), read as 'those he did not think inspired he called inspired'. Bracketed (οὖν) after εὐλόγως is an editorial supplement, rendered 'then'. Reviewer: τούτοις in 'ὄφιν τούτοις ἀντιπράσσοντα' refers back to the παραγγέλματα, so it is made explicit as 'these commandments'.
